title: Manage and control resources in a sustainable manner

lessons.title: What sustainable resource management means
lessons.html:
Farming for today and tomorrow

Sustainable resource management means using land, water, energy, biodiversity, people and money in a way that keeps the farm productive and profitable now without reducing the ability of future generations to farm. It rests on three pillars: environmental (soil, water, biodiversity), economic (profit and financial resilience) and social (workers, community, food security).

Farm resources to manage

ResourceSustainability concern
SoilErosion, compaction, organic matter loss, acidification
WaterOver-abstraction, pollution, wasteful irrigation
Veld and biodiversityOvergrazing, bush encroachment, alien invasive plants, loss of wetlands
EnergyHigh electricity and diesel costs, emissions, load-shedding
InputsOver-use of fertiliser and chemicals, waste
PeopleSkills, safety, fair treatment, retention
CapitalDebt levels, reinvestment

The legal framework

Several South African laws set minimum standards: the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 (soil, veld, alien plants), the National Water Act 36 of 1998 (lawful water use and pollution prevention), and the National Environmental Management Act 107 of 1998 with its duty of care to prevent significant environmental harm. Compliance is the starting point; sustainable management goes further.

Why it pays

Sustainable practices often reduce costs (less fertiliser, fuel and water), protect long-term yields, meet buyer and export requirements, and reduce risk from droughts and regulations. Many retailers and export markets now audit sustainability through schemes they specify.

lessons.title: Practical resource control on the farm
lessons.html:
Measure, manage, improve

You cannot manage what you do not measure. Set up simple monitoring for each key resource and assign responsibility.

Water

  • Install water meters on boreholes and irrigation lines; record use monthly.
  • Schedule irrigation with soil moisture probes or weather data rather than habit.
  • Fix leaks; maintain drippers and sprinklers for even distribution.
  • Harvest rainwater from roofs for sheds and homes.

Soil and veld

  • Use soil analysis-based fertilisation and conservation agriculture.
  • Match stocking rates to carrying capacity; rotate and rest camps.
  • Clear alien invasive plants such as wattle, prickly pear and lantana under a long-term plan with follow-up.
  • Protect wetlands and riparian zones.

Energy

  • Record electricity and diesel use per enterprise.
  • Service tractors and pumps for fuel efficiency; avoid unnecessary passes.
  • Consider solar pumps and panels, efficient lighting and variable-speed drives.

Waste

Reduce, reuse and recycle. Return empty agrochemical containers through approved collection schemes, compost organic waste, recycle plastics and oil, and keep waste away from water sources.

People

Invest in training, safe working conditions under the OHS Act 85 of 1993 and fair labour practices. Skilled, motivated workers use resources more carefully.

Example

A Limpopo citrus farm installs soil moisture probes and meters. It finds two blocks are over-irrigated by about a fifth. Adjusting schedules saves water and electricity and reduces nutrient leaching, with no loss in yield.

lessons.title: Planning, monitoring and reporting
lessons.html:
Building a sustainability management plan

Steps

  1. Baseline: record current use and condition of each resource (water use, energy use, soil analyses, veld condition, waste, staff turnover).
  2. Set targets that are specific and measurable, e.g. reduce water use per tonne of fruit by 10% in three years.
  3. Action plan: what will be done, by whom, by when and at what cost in ZAR.
  4. Monitor monthly or seasonally with indicators.
  5. Review annually and adjust.

Useful indicators

  • Water use per hectare and per unit of product.
  • kWh and litres of diesel per tonne produced.
  • Soil organic carbon trends.
  • Veld condition and ground cover.
  • Fertiliser and chemical use per hectare.
  • Lost-time injuries and staff turnover.
  • Profit per hectare and debt ratio.

Controlling resources

Controls include budgets, authorisation limits for purchases, issue registers for inputs, meters, regular inspections and clear responsibilities. Deviations from targets should trigger investigation: is the cause weather, equipment, people or the plan itself?

Reporting

Report results to owners, staff, buyers and certification bodies honestly. Recognise teams that achieve targets. Use the results to support applications for sustainability-linked markets or financing.

Key points

  • Sustainability balances environmental, economic and social goals.
  • Know the laws that set minimum standards: CARA, the National Water Act and NEMA.
  • Measure water, energy, soil, veld, waste and people indicators.
  • Set measurable targets and action plans with responsibilities.
  • Review and report results every year.
